Title [Dingbat](link_7) from an 1886 _Lampoon_

_**The Harvard Lampoon**_ is an [undergraduate](link_8)[humor publication](link_3) founded in 1876 by seven undergraduates at [Harvard University](link_5) in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts").

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Harvard_Lampoon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Overview")]

The _Harvard Lampoon_ publication was founded in 1876 by seven undergraduates at [Harvard University](link_5) in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), who were inspired by popular magazines like _[Punch](link_9)_ (1841) and _[Puck](link_10)_ (1876).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-2)_The Harvard Lampoon_ is the world's third longest-running continually published humor magazine, after the Swedish _[Blandaren](link_11)_ (1863) and the Swiss _[Nebelspalter](link_12)_ (1875).

The organization also produces occasional humor books (the best known being the 1969 [J. R. R. Tolkien](link_13) parody _[Bored of the Rings](link_14)_) and parodies of national magazines such as _[Entertainment Weekly](link_15)_ and _[Sports Illustrated](link_16)_. Much of the organization's capital is provided by the licensing of the "Lampoon" name to _[National Lampoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Lampoon,\_Inc [link_17]. "National Lampoon, Inc.")_, begun by _Harvard Lampoon_ graduates in 1970.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The _Lampoon_ publishes five issues annually. In 2006, the _Lampoon_ began regularly releasing content on its website, including pieces from the magazine and web-only content. In 2009, the _Lampoon_ published a parody of _[Twilight](link_18)_ called _Nightlight_, which is a _New York Times_ bestseller.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-3) In February 2012, the _Lampoon_ released a parody of _[The Hunger Games](link_19)_ called _[The Hunger Pains](link_20)_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-4) also a _New York Times_ bestseller.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-5)

The _Lampoon_ is housed a few blocks from [Harvard Square](link_21) in a mock-[Flemish](link_22) castle, the [Harvard Lampoon Building](link_1). It has been ranked by the magazine _[Complex](link_23)_ as the fifth most phallic building in the world.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-6)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Harvard_Lampoon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/HUPSF_Lampoon_Folder1_Image3_1885.jpg/250px-HUPSF_Lampoon_Folder1_Image3_1885.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HUPSF_Lampoon_Folder1_Image3_1885.jpg)

 The 1885 _Lampoon_ staff includes several notables, such as philosopher G. Santayana and newspaperman W.R. Hearst.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Santayana_image_Lampoon_XI_1886.jpg/250px-Santayana_image_Lampoon_XI_1886.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Santayana_image_Lampoon_XI_1886.jpg)

Cartoon by philosopher G. Santayana, Harvard class of 1886

The _Harvard Lampoon_ was first published in 1876 by seven founders including [Ralph Wormeley Curtis](link_24), [Edward Sandford Martin](link_25), [Edmund March Wheelwright](link_26), and Arthur Murray Sherwood[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-7) (father of [Robert E. Sherwood](link_27)).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-8) The first issue of the _Lampoon_ was a single copy, nailed to a tree in Harvard Yard. In its earliest years the magazine focused primarily on the satirization of Harvard and [Boston Brahmin](link_28) society. As the _Lampoon_ began to gain notoriety on campus, the society moved from offices in Hollis Hall to addresses on Holyoke and Plympton streets respectively. These collections of rooms rented by the trustees of the _Lampoon_ were famous not only for their beer nights, but also with the regularity that the _Lampoon_ spent the profits made on each magazine for these beer nights. "It was a good night when the Lampoon could afford coal and beer, and they often had to choose between one or the other." Pranks abounded in the early years, some more destructive than others. [William Randolph Hearst](link_29) was expelled from Harvard after sending a pudding pot used as a chamber pot to a professor.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-9)

A _Lampoon_ graduate from 1887, [Archibald Cary Coolidge](link_30), professor of architecture at Harvard College, was chosen as the architect of Randolph Hall, one of the college's newest dormitories. Legend has it that when designing Randolph, Coolidge purposefully made the dormitory recessed further back from Mt. Auburn Street than was at first designed, purchasing for himself the land the Castle now stands on.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The commission to design the castle was given to Edmund M. Wheelwright, then city architect of Boston.

The _Lampoon_ and its sensibility began to branch out away from the Harvard campus in the early 1960s, and soon became an important expression of, and feeder system for, American humor and comedy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 1961, _[Mademoiselle](link_31)_ offered the _Lampoon_ staff an honorarium to produce a parody of their own magazine for the traditionally lower-selling July issue. The project boosted _Mademoiselle'_ s summer circulation along with the _Lampoon_'s ever tenuous cash flow, and the magazine renewed its association with the _Lampoon_ for a follow-up parody in July 1962, and a third parody issue (of _[Esquire](link_32)_) in July 1963. The magazine also produced a 70-page spoof of [Ian Fleming](link_33)'s _[James Bond](link_34)_ novels in 1962 titled _Alligator,_ which was subsequently released by [Random House](link_35). These projects proved popular, and led to full, nationally-distributed parodies of _[Playboy](link_36)_ (1966), _[Time](link_37)_ (1968), and _[Life](link_38)_ (1969), and later, _[Cosmopolitan](link_39)_ in 1972, _[Sports Illustrated](link_16)_ (1974), and _[People](link_40)_ (1981).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Harvard_Lampoon#cite_note-10)

Cambridge (/ˈkeɪmbrɪdʒ/[3] KAYM-brij) is a city in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, United States. It is located in the Greater Boston metropolitan area directly across the Charles River from Boston. The city's population as of the 2020 U.S. census was 118,403, making it the most populous city in the county, the fourth-largest in Massachusetts behind Boston, Worcester, and Springfield, and ninth-most populous in New England.[4][5] The city was named in honor of the University of Cambridge in Cambridge, England, which was an important center of the Puritan theology that was embraced by the town's founders.[6]: 18 

Founded in December 1630 during the colonial era, Cambridge was one among the first cities established in the Thirteen Colonies, and it went on to play a historic role during the American Revolution. In May 1775, approximately 16,000 American patriots assembled in Cambridge Common to begin organizing a military retaliation against British troops following the Battles of Lexington and Concord. On July 2, 1775, two weeks after the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia formally established the Continental Army and appointed George Washington commander of it, Washington arrived at Cambridge Common to take command of the Patriot soldiers camped there. Many of these soldiers played a role in supporting Washington's successful siege of Boston, which trapped garrisoned British troops from moving by land, forcing the British to ultimately abandon Boston. Cambridge Common is thus celebrated as the birthplace of the Continental Army.[7][8]

Harvard University, an Ivy League university founded in Cambridge in 1636, is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), a private research university, has its 168-acre campus in Cambridge.[9]

Kendall Square, near MIT in the eastern part of Cambridge, has been called "the most innovative square mile on the planet" due to the high concentration of startup companies that have emerged there since 2010.[10] In 2022, Cambridge was home to over 250 biotech companies, with more than 120 located within the Kendall Square ZIP Code.[11]

Historyedit
For a chronological guide, see Timeline of Cambridge, Massachusetts.
George Washington takes command of the Continental Army in Cambridge Square on July 3, 1775; Cambridge is considered the birthplace of the Continental Army, which went on to secure American independence by defeating the British in the American Revolutionary War.
An 1873 map of Harvard Square
An 1873 map of Cambridge
An 1852 map of Greater Boston highlighting the regional rail lines and course of Middlesex Canal; Cambridge is near the bottom of the map highlighted in yellow, and West Cambridge, which is present-day Arlington, Massachusetts, highlighted in pink
Pre-colonizationedit

Native Americans inhabited the Charles River basin for thousands of years prior to European colonization of the Americas, as confirmed by archaeological remains in neighboring Watertown and Boston.[12] At the time of European contact, the area was inhabited by Naumkeag of the Pawtucket Confederacy to the north and Massachusett to the south.[13]

The contact period introduced a number of European infectious diseases which would decimate native populations in virgin soil epidemics, significantly depopulating the Charles River basin upon the arrival of large groups of English settlers in the 1630s.[12] A deed for the land that includes present-day Cambridge was ultimately obtained from the Naumkeag Squaw Sachem of Mistick in 1639,[14][15] after a leptospirosis epidemic in 1616–1619[16] and a smallpox epidemic in 1633 killed large portions of her tribe, including two of her sons.[17]

Some sources list Cambridge as the English toponym for Anmoughcawgen, meaning 'fishing weir' or 'beaver dam' in Natick,[18] however this misconception arises from John Smith's 1617 Description of New England,[13][19] in which Cambridge was one of several English place names arbitrarily applied by Smith and Prince Charles I of England,[20][19] in this case to a location on the Kennebec River in Maine,[20] far to the north of the later settlement of Cambridge, which was not so named until 1638.[21] An indigenous place name for the present day location of Cambridge is not known, though other native place names along the Charles in the 1600s included Pequoset and Nonantum upstream and Mishawum and Shawmut downstream,[12][22] while the Charles River (also named by Smith) was known as the Quinobequin.[18]

17th century and colonialismedit

The first settlement of the Massachusetts Bay Colony was established in Salem, in June 1626. That December, the site of present-day Cambridge was chosen for development because it was safely upriver from Boston Harbor, making it easily defensible from attacks by enemy ships. The city was founded by Thomas Dudley, his daughter Anne Bradstreet, and his son-in-law Simon Bradstreet. The first houses were built in the spring of 1631. The settlement was initially referred to as "the newe towne".[23][24] Official Massachusetts records show the name rendered as Newe Towne by 1632, and as Newtowne by 1638.[24][25]

Located at the first convenient Charles River crossing west of Boston, Newtowne was one of several towns, including Boston, Dorchester, Watertown, and Weymouth, founded by the 700 original Puritan colonists of the Massachusetts Bay Colony who arrived on the Winthrop Fleet. Its first preacher was Thomas Hooker, who led many of its original inhabitants west in 1636 to found Hartford and the Connecticut Colony; before leaving, they sold their plots to more recent immigrants from England.[23] The original village site is now within Harvard Square. The marketplace where farmers sold crops from surrounding towns at the edge of a salt marsh (since filled) remains within a small park at the corner of John F. Kennedy and Winthrop Streets.

In 1636, Newe College, later renamed Harvard College after benefactor John Harvard, was founded as North America's first institution of higher learning. Its initial purpose was training ministers. According to Cotton Mather, Newtowne was chosen for the site of the college by the Great and General Court, then the legislature of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, primarily for its proximity to the popular and highly respected Puritan preacher Thomas Shepard. In May 1638,[21] the settlement's name was changed to Cambridge in honor of the University of Cambridge in Cambridge, England.[23][26]

In 1639, the Great and General Court purchased the land that became present-day Cambridge from the Naumkeag Squaw Sachem of Mistick.[14][15]

The town comprised a much larger area than the present city,[23] with various outlying parts becoming independent towns over the years: Cambridge Village (later Newtown and now Newton) in 1688,[27] Cambridge Farms (now Lexington) in 1712[23] or 1713,[28] and Little or South Cambridge (now Brighton)[a] and Menotomy or West Cambridge (now Arlington) in 1807.[23][29][b] In the late 19th century, various schemes for annexing Cambridge to Boston were pursued and rejected.[30]

Newtowne's ministers, Hooker and Shepard, the college's first president, the college's major benefactor, and the first schoolmaster Nathaniel Eaton were all Cambridge alumni, as was the colony's governor John Winthrop. In 1629, Winthrop had led the signing of the founding document of the city of Boston, which was known as the Cambridge Agreement, after the university.[31] In 1650, Governor Thomas Dudley signed the charter creating the corporation that still governs Harvard College.[32]

Cambridge grew slowly as an agricultural village eight miles (13 km) by road from Boston, the colony's capital. By the American Revolution, most residents lived near the Common and Harvard College, with most of the town comprising farms and estates. Most inhabitants were descendants of the original Puritan colonists, but there was also a small elite of Anglican "worthies" who were not involved in village life, made their livings from estates, investments, and trade, and lived in mansions along "the Road to Watertown", present-day Brattle Street, which is still known as Tory Row.

18th century and Revolutionary Waredit

Newly appointed commander-in-chief of the Continental Army General George Washington, dispatched from the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia, arrived on July 3, 1775, and took command of the force of Patriot soldiers camped on Cambridge Common, today regarded as the birthplace of the American army.[23][c]

On January 24, 1776, Henry Knox arrived with an artillery train captured from Fort Ticonderoga, which allowed Washington to force the British Army to evacuate Boston. Most of the Loyalist estates in Cambridge were confiscated after the Revolutionary War.

19th century and industrializationedit

Between 1790 and 1840, Cambridge grew rapidly with the construction of West Boston Bridge in 1792 connecting Cambridge directly to Boston, making it no longer necessary to travel eight miles (13 km) through the Boston Neck, Roxbury, and Brookline to cross the Charles River. A second bridge, the Canal Bridge, opened in 1809 alongside the new Middlesex Canal. The new bridges and roads made what were formerly estates and marshland into prime industrial and residential districts.

In the mid-19th century, Cambridge was the center of a literary revolution. It was home to some of the famous Fireside poets, named because their poems would often be read aloud by families in front of their evening fires. The Fireside poets, including Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, James Russell Lowell, and Oliver Wendell Holmes, were highly popular and influential in this era.

Soon after, turnpikes were built: the Cambridge and Concord Turnpike (today's Broadway and Concord Ave.), the Middlesex Turnpike (Hampshire St. and Massachusetts Ave. northwest of Porter Square), and what are today's Cambridge, Main, and Harvard Streets connected various areas of Cambridge to the bridges. In addition, the town was connected to the Boston & Maine Railroad,[33] leading to the development of Porter Square as well as the creation of neighboring Somerville from the formerly rural parts of Charlestown.

Cambridge was incorporated as a city in 1846.[23] The city's commercial center began to shift from Harvard Square to Central Square, which became the city's downtown around that time.

Between 1850 and 1900, Cambridge took on much of its present character, featuring streetcar suburban development along the turnpikes and working class and industrial neighborhoods focused on East Cambridge, comfortable middle-class housing on the old Cambridgeport, and Mid-Cambridge estates and upper-class enclaves near Harvard University and on the minor hills. The arrival of the railroad in North Cambridge and Northwest Cambridge led to three changes: the development of massive brickyards and brickworks between Massachusetts Avenue, Concord Avenue, and Alewife Brook; the ice-cutting industry launched by Frederic Tudor on Fresh Pond; and the carving up of the last estates into residential subdivisions to house the thousands of immigrants who arrived to work in the new industries.

For much of the 19th and early 20th centuries, the city's largest employer was the New England Glass Company, founded in 1818. By the middle of the 19th century, it was the world's largest and most modern glassworks. In 1888, Edward Drummond Libbey moved all production to Toledo, Ohio, where it continues today under the name Owens-Illinois. The company's flint glassware with heavy lead content is prized by antique glass collectors, and the Toledo Museum of Art has a large collection. The Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and the Sandwich Glass Museum on Cape Cod also house several pieces.

In 1895, Edwin Ginn, founder of Ginn and Company, built the Athenaeum Press Building for his publishing textbook empire.

20th centuryedit

By 1920, Cambridge was one of New England's main industrial cities, with nearly 120,000 residents. Among the largest businesses in Cambridge during the period of industrialization was Carter's Ink Company, whose neon sign long adorned the Charles River and which was for many years the world's largest ink manufacturer. Next door was the Athenaeum Press. Confectionery and snack manufacturers in the Cambridgeport-Area 4-Kendall corridor included Kennedy Biscuit Factory, later part of Nabisco and originator of the Fig Newton,[34] Necco, Squirrel Brands,[35] George Close Company (1861–1930s),[36] Page & Shaw, Daggett Chocolate (1892–1960s, recipes bought by Necco),[37] Fox Cross Company (1920–1980, originator of the Charleston Chew, and now part of Tootsie Roll Industries),[38] Kendall Confectionery Company, and James O. Welch (1927–1963, originator of Junior Mints, Sugar Daddies, Sugar Mamas, and Sugar Babies, now part of Tootsie Roll Industries).[39] Main Street was nicknamed "Confectioner's Row".[40]

Only the Cambridge Brands subsidiary of Tootsie Roll Industries remains in town, still manufacturing Junior Mints in the old Welch factory on Main Street.[39] The Blake and Knowles Steam Pump Company (1886), the Kendall Boiler and Tank Company (1880, now in Chelmsford, Massachusetts), and the New England Glass Company (1818–1878) were among the industrial manufacturers in what are now Kendall Square and East Cambridge.

In 1935, the Cambridge Housing Authority and the Public Works Administration demolished an integrated low-income tenement neighborhood with African Americans and European immigrants. In its place, it built the whites-only "Newtowne Court" public housing development and the adjoining, blacks-only "Washington Elms" project in 1940; the city required segregation in its other public housing projects as well.[41][42][43]

As industry in New England began to decline during the Great Depression and after World War II, Cambridge lost much of its industrial base. It also began to become an intellectual, rather than an industrial, center. Harvard University, which had always been important as both a landowner and an institution, began to play a more dominant role in the city's life and culture. When Radcliffe College was established in 1879, the town became a mecca for some of the nation's most academically talented female students. MIT's move from Boston to Cambridge in 1916 reinforced Cambridge's status as an intellectual center of the United States.

After the 1950s, the city's population began to decline slowly as families tended to be replaced by single people and young couples. In Cambridge Highlands, the technology company Bolt, Beranek, & Newman produced the first network router in 1969 and hosted the invention of computer-to-computer email in 1971. The 1980s brought a wave of high technology startups. Those selling advanced minicomputers were overtaken by the microcomputer.[citation needed][44] Cambridge-based VisiCorp made the first spreadsheet software for personal computers, VisiCalc, and helped propel the Apple II to consumer success. It was overtaken and purchased by Cambridge-based Lotus Development, maker of Lotus 1-2-3 (which was, in turn, replaced in by Microsoft Excel).

## From today's featured article

[![Image 6: Pennsylvania State Capitol](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Flying_the_Pride_Flag_over_the_Capitol_%2850035197647%29.jpg/250px-Flying_the_Pride_Flag_over_the_Capitol_%2850035197647%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flying_the_Pride_Flag_over_the_Capitol_(50035197647).jpg "Pennsylvania State Capitol")

The **[Pennsylvania State Capitol](link_33)** is located in [Harrisburg](link_21). The building was designed by [Joseph Miller Huston](link_22) and completed in 1906 in a [Beaux-Arts](link_23) style with decorative [Renaissance](link_24) themes. It houses the legislative chambers for the [Pennsylvania General Assembly](link_25), the Harrisburg chambers for the [Supreme Court](link_26) and [Superior Court of Pennsylvania](link_27), and the offices of [the state's governor](link_28) and [lieutenant governor](link_29). The capitol project was the subject of a [graft](link_30) scandal, as the construction and furnishing cost three times more than the General Assembly had appropriated for the project. The Pennsylvania State Capitol is often referred to as a "palace of art" because of its many sculptures, murals, and stained-glass windows, most of which are Pennsylvania-themed or were made in Pennsylvania. The building was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](link_31) in 1977 and designated a [National Historic Landmark](link_32) in 2006. _(**[Full article...](link_33)**)_

## Did you know...

[![Image 7: Ernst Frey](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Ernst_Frey.jpg/250px-Ernst_Frey.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ernst_Frey.jpg "Ernst Frey")

Ernst Frey

*   ... that **[a man born in Austria](link_38)**_(pictured)_ became one of the first colonels of the People's Army of Vietnam?
*   ... that the melodies of _**[Alarms in the Heart](link_39)**_ were likened to Gregorian chants?
*   ... that Australian model **[Cindy Rostron](link_40)** also had a career as an Indigenous ranger?
*   ... that from 1959 all Guinean people aged 7 to 35 years old statutorily belonged to the **[Youth of the African Democratic Revolution](link_41)**?
*   ... that **[Grady Prestage](link_42)** was the first African American elected to the [Fort Bend County](link_43) commissioners' court since Reconstruction?
*   ... that John James Audubon gave his wife ownership of **[his Manhattan estate](link_44)** to prevent debt collectors from seizing it?
*   ... that **[Philoxenos Yuhanon Dolabani](link_45)** defied church policy against Assyrian nationalism through anonymous poetry?
*   ... that the anthropomorphic skunk **[Sabrina](link_46)** has been called "one of the most famous [furry](link_47) comics stars"?
*   ... that drag queen **[Marcus Hunter-Neill](link_48)** once donated £20,000 worth of clothes to charity?

**Harvard Square** is a triangular plaza at the intersection of [Massachusetts Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Avenue_(Boston) "Massachusetts Avenue (Boston)"), [Brattle Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brattle_Street_(Cambridge,_Massachusetts) "Brattle Street (Cambridge, Massachusetts)"), and John F. Kennedy Street near the center of [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), United States. The term "Harvard Square" is also used to delineate the business district and [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") surrounding that intersection, which is the historic center of Cambridge.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square#cite_note-urlMACRIS.CAM.AB_Details-2) Adjacent to [Harvard Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard "Harvard Yard"), the historic heart of [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square#cite_note-urlMACRIS.CAM.AD_Details-3) the Square (as it is sometimes called, locally) functions as a commercial center for Harvard students, as well as residents of western Cambridge, the western and northern neighborhoods and the inner suburbs of [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). The Square is served by [Harvard station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_(MBTA_station) "Harvard (MBTA station)"), a major [MBTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority")[Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_(MBTA) "Red Line (MBTA)")[subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") station and a bus [transportation hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_hub "Transportation hub").

The name "Harvard Square" can also refer to the entire neighborhood surrounding this intersection for several blocks in each direction, including Brattle Square, a block away, and the nearby [Cambridge Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Common "Cambridge Common"). The Common is a park area with a playground, baseball field, and a number of monuments, several relating to the [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War").

## Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harvard_Square&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Location")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Harvard_Square_aerial_1.JPG/330px-Harvard_Square_aerial_1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harvard_Square_aerial_1.JPG)

Aerial view of the Mass Ave/Brattle Street junction, with Harvard Yard at the right, looking north

The center of Harvard Square is the junction of [Massachusetts Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Avenue_(Boston) "Massachusetts Avenue (Boston)") and [Brattle Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brattle_Street_(Cambridge,_Massachusetts) "Brattle Street (Cambridge, Massachusetts)"). Massachusetts Avenue enters from the southeast, a few miles after crossing the [Charles River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River "Charles River") from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") near the [MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") campus, and turns sharply north at the intersection. Brattle Street and John F. Kennedy Street merge from the southwest and join Massachusetts Avenue at that point. The area is dominated by a large pedestrian space that includes the MBTA [subway headhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headhouse#Subways "Headhouse") (entrance) and the historic [Harvard Square Subway Kiosk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square_Subway_Kiosk "Harvard Square Subway Kiosk"), which formerly housed the _Out of Town News_ newsstand.

The main building of the [Harvard/MIT Cooperative Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard/MIT_Cooperative_Society "Harvard/MIT Cooperative Society") forms part of the western side of the intersection, along with a bank and several retail shops; on the eastern side is the walled enclosure of [Harvard Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard "Harvard Yard").

### Nearby places

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harvard_Square&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Nearby places")]

The core of the campus of [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") lies in the vicinity of Harvard Square, including Harvard Yard as well as the [Harvard Extension School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Extension_School "Harvard Extension School"), the [Harvard Art Museums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Art_Museums "Harvard Art Museums"), the [Semitic Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Semitic_Museum "Harvard Semitic Museum"), the [Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Museum_of_Archaeology_and_Ethnology "Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology"), and the [Harvard Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Museum_of_Natural_History "Harvard Museum of Natural History").

Other institutions in the surrounding area include the [Cambridge Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Public_Library "Cambridge Public Library"), [Lesley University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesley_University "Lesley University"), the [Longy School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longy_School_of_Music "Longy School of Music"), the [Episcopal Divinity School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Divinity_School "Episcopal Divinity School"), the [Cambridge Rindge and Latin School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Rindge_and_Latin_School "Cambridge Rindge and Latin School"), the [American Repertory Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Repertory_Theater "American Repertory Theater"), the [Cooper-Frost-Austin House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper-Frost-Austin_House "Cooper-Frost-Austin House"), the [Hooper-Lee-Nichols House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooper-Lee-Nichols_House "Hooper-Lee-Nichols House"), and the [Longfellow House–Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longfellow_House%E2%80%93Washington's_Headquarters_National_Historic_Site "Longfellow House–Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site").

Due to its high pedestrian traffic, Harvard Square and nearby Brattle Square (the intersection of Brattle St. and Mt. Auburn St.) serve as gathering places for street musicians and [buskers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busker "Busker"). Singer-songwriter [Tracy Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Chapman "Tracy Chapman"), who attended nearby [Tufts University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tufts_University "Tufts University"), performed there during her college years. [Amanda Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Palmer "Amanda Palmer"), a member of [the Dresden Dolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dresden_Dolls "The Dresden Dolls"), also performed in the square as a "[living statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_statue "Living statue")".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square#cite_note-Lotman-4) Other performers who have appeared there include indie rock guitarist [Mary Lou Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Lou_Lord "Mary Lou Lord") and the juggling

**Ernst Frey** (10 June 1915 – 13 January 1994), also known as **Nguyễn Dân** and **Hồ Chí Dân**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-1)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-2) was an Austrian soldier who served in the [French Foreign Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Foreign_Legion "French Foreign Legion") before defecting to the [Vietnam People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_People's_Army "Vietnam People's Army"). Frey commanded the [4th Military Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Military_Region "4th Military Region"), [9th Military Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_Military_Region_(Vietnam_People's_Army) "9th Military Region (Vietnam People's Army)"), and was among the first colonels of the Vietnam People's Army. During the [First Indochina War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Indochina_War "First Indochina War"), he served as an assistant to [Võ Nguyên Giáp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%B5_Nguy%C3%AAn_Gi%C3%A1p "Võ Nguyên Giáp"), the then-Minister of Defense of [North Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam "North Vietnam") and then-Commander-in-Chief of the Vietnam People's Army.

Born in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") in 1915, Frey became involved in the Austrian communist movement as a teenager and was imprisoned several times for his political activities. In 1938, he fled Austria and joined the French Foreign Legion, serving in Algeria and later [French Indochina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Indochina "French Indochina"). In French Indochina, he established a communist group with some Legion members, in turn joining the [Indochinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochinese_Communist_Party "Indochinese Communist Party"). After the [August Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Revolution "August Revolution") in 1945, he took part in the Vietnamese revolutionary movement against the French. In 1951, Frey returned to Austria, where he spent a short time serving in the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") and the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Greens_(Austria) "The Greens (Austria)") before dying in 1994.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ernst_Frey&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Ernst Frey was born on 10 June 1915, in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), Austria-Hungary, into a family of Hungarian and [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") origin. His father was a Jewish [social democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democracy "Social democracy") and was serving in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:0-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4) In his teenage years, Frey participated in the Socialist High School Youth Association (VSM). In 1934, he joined the Austrian Communist Youth League. Due to his activities in the VSM and accusations of treason, Frey was imprisoned multiple times and banned from attending Austrian universities.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:0-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4) He was later released on July 1936 and had a job at [Bunzl & Biach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunzl "Bunzl").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:2-5)

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ernst_Frey&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

In 1938, Austria was [annexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anschluss "Anschluss") by Nazi Germany, and German troops entered Vienna. Frey's mother was captured and publicly tortured.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:2-5) Frey subsequently emigrated and planned to join the [International Brigades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Brigades "International Brigades") of the [Spanish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Spanish_Republic "Second Spanish Republic") in the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War"). However, he was captured by the [Schutzstaffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutzstaffel "Schutzstaffel") and spent three months in prison before the German authorities revoked his citizenship.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4) Fleeing to Switzerland, he was also imprisoned for several months.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:3-6) After being released, he escaped to France to continue his way to Spain. In [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), Frey made a living by selling pencils. After being refused permission to travel to Spain, he remained in France and joined the French Foreign Legion, where he was deployed to Algeria.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:0-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4)

In 1940, believing that his opportunity to fight against Nazi Germany had passed, Frey volunteered to serve in French Indochina, hoping that the ship transporting him would be intercepted by the British, giving him an opportunity to fight against Nazi Germany on the British side.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:5-7) Frey was assigned to the [5th Foreign Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_Foreign_Infantry_Regiment "5th Foreign Infantry Regiment").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-8) In 1941, the ship arrived to Saigon without being attacked even once,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:5-7) and Frey began organizing a small group of communists in the Foreign Legion in [Việt Trì](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vi%E1%BB%87t_Tr%C3%AC_city "Việt Trì city"). Dissatisfied with France's cooperation with the [Empire of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") and the [Axis powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers"), the group sought to establish contact with French socialists in [Hanoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanoi "Hanoi"). They also tried to talk to local people in Việt Trì, but were often unsuccessful. Their goal was to join forces with the local French resistance in order to connect with the [Indochinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochinese_Communist_Party "Indochinese Communist Party") and [Viet Minh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viet_Minh "Viet Minh").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4)

In 1943, an Austrian member of Frey's group established contact with the Socialist Party in Hanoi, which enabled them to engage directly with members of the Communist Party. By the end of 1943, Frey had his first meeting with Túc, an envoy from the Central Executive Committee of the Party. As a result, his communist group chose to apply for membership in the Indochinese Communist Party. After Túc's guidance, Frey received assistance and education from [Trường Chinh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C6%B0%E1%BB%9Dng_Chinh "Trường Chinh"), the [Party's General Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Communist_Party_of_Vietnam "General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam") (at the time, Trường Chinh was using the codename "Phong"). Supported by Trường Chinh, Frey was accepted into the Indochinese Communist Party on his 29th birthday in 1944.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:4-9) His communist cell was also admitted into the Party later that year.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4)

### Service in Viet Minh

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ernst_Frey&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Service in Viet Minh")]

Following the [Japanese coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_in_French_Indochina "Japanese coup d'état in French Indochina") on 9 March 1945, Frey and his comrades were held in an extermination camp, where they suffered from [dysentery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysentery "Dysentery") and [malaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria "Malaria").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Frey#cite_note-:1-4) They were then released after the

This article contains information about the literary events and publications of **1876**.

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1876_in_literature&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Events")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Arbo-Per_Gynt.jpg/250px-Arbo-Per_Gynt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arbo-Per_Gynt.jpg)

[Per Gynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_Gynt "Per Gynt"), the hero of the folk-story that [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen") loosely based _[Peer Gynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer\_Gynt "Peer Gynt")_ on

*   [February 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_24 "February 24") – The stage premiere of the verse-play _[Peer Gynt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer\_Gynt "Peer Gynt")_ by [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen") (published [1867](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1867_in_literature "1867 in literature")) with incidental music by [Edvard Grieg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvard_Grieg "Edvard Grieg"), takes place in [Christiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo"), Norway.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-1)
*   February/March – _[The Harvard Lampoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Harvard\_Lampoon "The Harvard Lampoon")_ humor magazine is founded in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts").
*   [March 14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_14 "March 14") – [Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Roma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioteca_Nazionale_Centrale_di_Roma "Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Roma") established in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").
*   March 
    *   [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans") librarian [Melvil Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvil_Dewey "Melvil Dewey") first publishes the [Dewey Decimal Classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Decimal_Classification "Dewey Decimal Classification") system.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-2)
    *   [George Bernard Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Bernard_Shaw "George Bernard Shaw") moves permanently from [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin") to England, after which he begins his writing career as the [ghostwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostwriter "Ghostwriter") of a musical column in London satirical weekly _The Hornet_.

*   April – [Émile Zola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Zola "Émile Zola")'s _[L'Assommoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Assommoir "L'Assommoir")_ begins serialization in _Le Bien public_. Its low-life themes cause it to be suspended after six episodes; serialization resumes in July in _La République des lettres_.
*   [May 30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_30 "May 30") – The [Ems Ukaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_Ukaz "Ems Ukaz"), a secret decree, is issued by Tsar [Alexander II of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_II_of_Russia "Alexander II of Russia") in the German city of [Bad Ems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Ems "Bad Ems"), aimed at stopping the printing and distribution of [Ukrainian-language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_language "Ukrainian language") publications in the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-3)
*   May – [April Uprising of 1876](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Uprising_of_1876 "April Uprising of 1876"): [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_poetry "Bulgarian poetry") poet [Hristo Botev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hristo_Botev "Hristo Botev") leads a party of émigré revolutionaries against Ottoman forces in Bulgaria but is shot and killed on June 1 (May 20 [O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style_and_New_Style_dates "Old Style and New Style dates")).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-4)
*   July – William Heffer takes over his first bookshop in [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge") (England), primarily as a stationer at this date.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-5)
*   [October 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_6 "October 6") – The [American Library Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Library_Association "American Library Association") is founded in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia").
*   December – The first United States edition of [Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain "Mark Twain")'s first individual extended work of fiction, the _[Bildungsroman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bildungsroman "Bildungsroman")_ _[The Adventures of Tom Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Adventures\_of\_Tom\_Sawyer "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer")_, illustrated by [True Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_Williams "True Williams"), is published by the [American Publishing Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Publishing_Company "American Publishing Company"). An authorised non-illustrated British edition has appeared in early June from [Chatto & Windus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatto_&_Windus "Chatto & Windus") in London (with the first review appearing on June 24 in a British magazine) and pirated editions have appeared in Canada and Germany.
*   _unknown dates_
    *   The first ([1594](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1594_in_literature "1594 in literature")) edition of [Christopher Marlowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe "Christopher Marlowe")'s play _[Edward II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward\_II\_(play) "Edward II (play)")_ is discovered.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-6)
    *   The [Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_des_Bouffes_du_Nord "Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord") opens in Paris.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_in_literature#cite_note-7)

**Oslo**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-13) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and [most populous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_towns_and_cities_in_Norway "List of towns and cities in Norway") city of [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"). It constitutes both a [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counties_of_Norway "Counties of Norway") and a [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities_of_Norway "Municipalities of Norway"). The municipality of Oslo had a population of 724,290 in 2025, while the city's greater [urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area") had a population of 1,110,887 in 2025,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-SSB-2023-14) and the [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") had an estimated population of 1,546,706 in 2021.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-regjeringen2010-15)

During the [Viking Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age "Viking Age"), the area was part of [Viken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viken_(region) "Viken (region)"). Oslo was founded as a city at the end of the Viking Age in 1040 under the name **Ánslo**, and established as a [_kaupstad_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kjobstad "Kjobstad") or trading place in 1048 by [Harald Hardrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Hardrada "Harald Hardrada"). The city was elevated to a [bishopric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Oslo "Diocese of Oslo") in 1070 and a capital under [Haakon V of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haakon_V_of_Norway "Haakon V of Norway") around the year 1300. [Personal unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") with [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") from [1397 to 1523](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmar_Union "Kalmar Union") and again from [1536 to 1814](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark%E2%80%93Norway "Denmark–Norway") reduced its influence. After being destroyed by a fire in 1624, during the reign of [King Christian IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_IV_of_Denmark "Christian IV of Denmark"), a new city was built closer to [Akershus Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akershus_Fortress "Akershus Fortress") and named **Christiania** in honour of the king. It became a [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_of_Norway "List of municipalities of Norway") (_[formannskapsdistrikt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formannskapsdistrikt "Formannskapsdistrikt")_) on 1 January 1838. The city functioned as the capital of Norway during the 1814–1905 [union between Sweden and Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_between_Sweden_and_Norway "Union between Sweden and Norway"). From 1877, the city's name was spelled **Kristiania** in government usage, a spelling that was adopted by the municipal authorities in 1897, although 'Christiania' was also used. In 1925, the city, after incorporating the village retaining its former name, was [renamed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#1900%E2%80%93present) 'Oslo'. In 1948, Oslo merged with [Aker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker,_Norway "Aker, Norway"), a municipality which surrounded the capital and which was 27 times larger, thus creating the modern, much larger Oslo municipality.

Oslo is the [economic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Norway "Economy of Norway") and [governmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Norway "Politics of Norway") centre of Norway. The city is also a hub of Norwegian trade, banking, industry and shipping. It is an important centre for maritime industries and [maritime trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_trade "Maritime trade") in Europe. The city is home to many companies within the maritime sector, some of which are among the world's largest shipping companies, shipbrokers and maritime insurance brokers. Oslo is a pilot city of the [Council of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Europe "Council of Europe") and the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") intercultural cities programme.

Oslo is considered a [global city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_city "Global city") and was ranked as a "Beta World City" by the [Globalization and World Cities Research Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network") in 2008.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-16) It was ranked number one in terms of quality of life among European large cities in the European Cities of the Future 2012 report by _fDi_ magazine.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-fdiintelligence.com-17) A survey conducted by [ECA International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECA_International "ECA International") in 2011 placed Oslo as the second most expensive city in the world for living expenses after [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-18) In 2013, Oslo tied with the [Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") city of [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") as the fourth most expensive city in the world, according to the [Economist Intelligence Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist_Intelligence_Unit "Economist Intelligence Unit")'s Worldwide Cost of Living study.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-19)

Oslo's population was increasing at record rates during the early 2000s, making it the fastest growing major [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") in Europe at the time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-20) This growth originates primarily from international [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_to_Norway "Immigration to Norway") and related high birth rates, but also from intra-national migration. By 2010 the immigrant population in the city was growing somewhat faster than the [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegians "Norwegians") population,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-21) and in the city proper this had become more than 25% of the total population if the children of immigrant parents were included.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-Immigration-22)

## Urban region

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Urban region")]

See also: [List of boroughs of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_boroughs_of_Oslo "List of boroughs of Oslo")

The municipality of Oslo has a population of 724,290 as of 1 January 2025.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-auto-23) The urban area extends far beyond the boundaries of the municipality into the surrounding [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counties_of_Norway "Counties of Norway") of [Akershus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akershus "Akershus") (municipalities of [Asker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asker "Asker"), [Bærum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A6rum "Bærum"), [Lillestrøm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillestr%C3%B8m_Municipality "Lillestrøm Municipality"), [Enebakk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enebakk "Enebakk"), [Rælingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A6lingen "Rælingen"), [Lørenskog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%B8renskog "Lørenskog"), [Nittedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nittedal "Nittedal"), [Gjerdrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gjerdrum "Gjerdrum"), [Nordre Follo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordre_Follo "Nordre Follo")); being, to a great degree suburbs of Oslo making up approximately 500,000 of the population of the [greater Oslo region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Oslo_Region "Greater Oslo Region"). The total population of this [agglomeration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agglomerations "Agglomerations") was 1,546,706 in 2023.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-SSB-2023-14) The city centre is situated at the end of the [Oslofjord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslofjord "Oslofjord"), from which point the city sprawls out in three distinct "corridors"—inland north-eastwards, and southwards along both sides of the fjord—which gives the [urbanized area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area") a shape reminiscent of an upside-down reclining "Y" (on maps, satellite pictures, or from high above the city).

To the north and east, wide forested hills (_Marka_) rise above the city giving the location the shape of a giant [amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre "Amphitheatre"). The urban [municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_of_Norway "List of municipalities of Norway") (_bykommune_) of Oslo and county (_[fylke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counties\_of\_Norway "Counties of Norway")_) of Oslo are two parts of the same entity, making Oslo the only city in Norway where two administrative levels are integrated. Of Oslo's total area, 130 km 2 (50 sq mi) is built-up and 9.6 km 2 (3.7 sq mi) is agricultural. The open areas within the built-up zone amount to 22 km 2 (8.5 sq mi).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-24)

The city of Oslo was established as a municipality on 3 January 1838 (see [formannskapsdistrikt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formannskapsdistrikt "Formannskapsdistrikt")). It was separated from the county of [Akershus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akershus "Akershus") to become a county of its own in 1842. The rural municipality of [Aker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker,_Norway "Aker, Norway") was merged with Oslo on 1 January 1948 (and simultaneously transferred from Akershus county to Oslo county). Furthermore, Oslo shares several important functions with Akershus county.
