## Name and seal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Name and seal")]

After being destroyed by a fire in 1624, during the reign of [King Christian IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_IV_of_Denmark "Christian IV of Denmark"), a new city was built closer to [Akershus Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akershus_Fortress "Akershus Fortress") and named Christiania in the king's honour. The old site east of the Aker river was not abandoned, however, and the village of Oslo remained as a suburb outside the city gates. The suburb called Oslo was eventually included in the city proper. In 1925 the name of the suburb was [transferred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#1900%E2%80%93present) to the whole city, while the suburb was renamed "[Gamlebyen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town,_Oslo "Old Town, Oslo")", literally "the Old town", to avoid confusion.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-Osloby-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-SNL_Historie-30) The Old Town is an area within the administrative district [Gamle Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamle_Oslo "Gamle Oslo"). The previous names are reflected in street names like Oslo gate (Oslo street)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-31) and Oslo hospital.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-32)

### Toponymy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Toponymy")]

For full article, see [History of Oslo's name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Oslo's_name "History of Oslo's name")

The origin of the name _Oslo_ has been the subject of much debate. It is almost certainly derived from [Old Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse "Old Norse") and was—in all probability—originally the name of a large farm at [Bjørvika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bj%C3%B8rvika "Bjørvika"), while the meaning of that name is disputed. Modern linguists generally interpret the original _Óslo_, _Áslo_ or _Ánslo_ as either "meadow at the foot of a hill" or "meadow consecrated to the [Gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86sir "Æsir")", with both considered equally likely.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-33)

Erroneously, it was once assumed that _Oslo_ meant "the mouth of the Lo river", a supposed previous name for the [river Alna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alnaelva "Alnaelva"). Not only has no evidence been found of a river "Lo" predating the work where [Peder Claussøn Friis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peder_Clauss%C3%B8n_Friis "Peder Claussøn Friis") first proposed this etymology, but the very name is ungrammatical in Norwegian: the correct form would have been _Loaros_ (cf. [Nidaros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nidaros "Nidaros")).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-34) The name _Lo_ is now believed to be a [back-formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back-formation "Back-formation") arrived at by Friis in support of his [idea about] etymology for _Oslo_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-35)

### Seal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Seal")]

Main article: [Seal of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_of_Oslo "Seal of Oslo")

Oslo is one of very few cities in Norway, besides [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen "Bergen") and [Tønsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%B8nsberg "Tønsberg"), that does not have a formal [coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms"), but which uses a city seal instead.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-36) The seal of Oslo shows the city's [patron saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron_saint "Patron saint"), [St. Hallvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallvard_Vebj%C3%B8rnsson "Hallvard Vebjørnsson"), with his attributes, the [millstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millstone "Millstone") and [arrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrow "Arrow"), with a naked woman at his feet. He is seated on a throne with lion decorations, which at the time was also commonly used by the [Norwegian kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Norwegian_monarchs "List of Norwegian monarchs").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-Heraldry-37)

### Other names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Other names")]

Oslo has various nicknames and names in other languages. The city is sometimes known as "The Tiger City" ([Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): _Tigerstaden_), probably inspired by an 1870 poem by [Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bj%C3%B8rnstjerne_Bj%C3%B8rnson "Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson") which referenced then-Christiania in central Oslo. The nickname is mostly used by Norwegians from out of town, and rarely by people from the Oslo region.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-38)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: History")]

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Oslo "Timeline of Oslo").

### Viking Age

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Viking Age")]

During the [Viking Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age "Viking Age"), the area that includes modern Oslo was located in [Viken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viken,_Norway "Viken, Norway"), the northernmost province of [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark"). Control over the area shifted between Danish and Norwegian kings in the Middle Ages, and Denmark continued to claim the area until 1241.

According to the Norse [sagas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga "Saga"), Oslo was founded around 1049 by [Harald Hardrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Hardrada "Harald Hardrada").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-39) Recent archaeological research, however, uncovered Christian burials which could be dated to prior to AD 1000, evidence of a preceding urban settlement.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-40) This called for the celebration of Oslo's millennium in 2000 rather than 2049.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1000–1600

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1000–1600")]

Main article: [Old Town, Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town,_Oslo "Old Town, Oslo")

Under the reign of [Olaf III of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olaf_III_of_Norway "Olaf III of Norway") (1067–1093), Oslo became a cultural centre for [Eastern Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Norway "Eastern Norway"). [Hallvard Vebjørnsson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallvard_Vebj%C3%B8rnsson "Hallvard Vebjørnsson") became the city's [patron saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron_saint "Patron saint") and is depicted on the city's seal.

In 1174, [Hovedøya Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoved%C3%B8ya_Abbey "Hovedøya Abbey") was built. The churches and abbeys became major owners of large tracts of land, which proved important for the city's economic development, especially before the Black Death.

At the end of the 12th century, [Hanseatic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanseatic_League "Hanseatic League") traders from [Rostock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostock "Rostock") moved into the city and gained major influence in the city.

On 25 July 1197, [Sverre of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sverre_of_Norway "Sverre of Norway") and his soldiers attacked Oslo from [Hovedøya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoved%C3%B8ya "Hovedøya").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-AttackFromHoved%C3%B8ya-41)

During the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), Oslo reached new heights during the reign of [Haakon V of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haakon_V_of_Norway "Haakon V of Norway") (1299–1319). He was the first king to reside permanently in the city, and it has been regarded as the capital city of Norway since his reign. He also started the construction of the [Akershus Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akershus_Fortress "Akershus Fortress") and the Oslo [Kongsgård](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kongsg%C3%A5rd "Kongsgård").

The Black Death came to Norway in 1349 and, like other cities in Europe, the city suffered greatly. The churches' earnings from their land dropped so much that the Hanseatic traders dominated the city's foreign trade in the 15th century.

In 1380, Norway was the weaker part in a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") with Denmark, and Oslo's role was reduced to that of provincial administrative centre, with the monarchs residing in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen").

### 17th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 17th century")]

Over the years, fires destroyed significant parts of the city multiple times, as many of the city's buildings were built entirely of wood. After the fourteenth calamity, in 1624, which lasted for three days, [Christian IV of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_IV_of_Denmark "Christian IV of Denmark") decided that the old city should not be rebuilt again. His men built a network of roads on the other side of the bay in Akershagen near [Akershus Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akershus_Castle "Akershus Castle"). He demanded that all citizens move their shops and workplaces to the newly built city of "Christiania", named in his honour.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-42) The part of the city built starting in 1624 is now often called _Kvadraturen[[Wikidata](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q11982577 "d:Special:EntityPage/Q11982577")]_ because of its orthogonal layout in regular, square blocks.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-43)[Anatomigården](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomig%C3%A5rden "Anatomigården") is a historic timber framing house located on the north side of Christiania Torv; it was built in 1640.

The transformation of Christiania went slowly for the first hundred years. However, outside of the city at [Vaterland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaterland,_Norway "Vaterland, Norway"), [Grønland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B8nland,_Oslo "Grønland, Oslo"), and the [old town of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town,_Oslo "Old Town, Oslo"), a new, unmanaged part of the city arose populated by citizens of lower class status.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The last [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death") outbreak in Oslo occurred in 1654.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-44)

### 18th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 18th century")]

In the 18th century, after the [Great Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_War "Great Northern War"), the city's economy boomed with shipbuilding and trade. The strong economy transformed Christiania into a trading port.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 19th century")]

The Royal Frederick University (now the [University of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oslo "University of Oslo")) was founded in 1811; the fact that it was founded this late reportedly had an adverse effect on the development of the nation.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-45)

[![Image 24: Royal Palace](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Royal_Palace%2C_Oslo_%282015%29.JPG/250px-Royal_Palace%2C_Oslo_%282015%29.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Royal_Palace,_Oslo_(2015).JPG)

Royal Palace, Oslo (2015)

In 1814 the former provincial town of Christiania became the capital of the independent Kingdom of Norway, when the union with Denmark was dissolved and replaced by a [personal union with Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_between_Sweden_and_Norway "Union between Sweden and Norway"). Several state institutions were established and the city's role as a capital initiated a period of rapidly increasing population. The government of this new state needed buildings for its expanding administration and institutions. Several important buildings and landmarks were erected in the 19th century, including the [Royal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace,_Oslo "Royal Palace, Oslo") (1825–1848), the [Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Stock_Exchange "Oslo Stock Exchange") (1826–1828), the [Bank of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Norway "Bank of Norway") (1828), the [Storting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storting "Storting") (1861–1866), the [National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Theatre_(Oslo) "National Theatre (Oslo)") (1899), and several [University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oslo "University of Oslo") buildings. Among the world-famous artists who lived here during this period were [Henrik Ibsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrik_Ibsen "Henrik Ibsen") and [Knut Hamsun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knut_Hamsun "Knut Hamsun") (the latter was awarded the Nobel Prize for literature).

Large areas of the surrounding [Aker municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker,_Norway "Aker, Norway") were incorporated in 1839, 1859, and 1878. The 1859 expansion included [Grünerløkka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%BCnerl%C3%B8kka "Grünerløkka"), [Grønland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%B8nland,_Oslo "Grønland, Oslo"), and [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town,_Oslo "Old Town, Oslo"). At that time the area called _Oslo_ (now _Gamlebyen_ or Old Town) was a village or suburb outside the city borders east of Aker river.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-46) The population increased from approximately 10.000 in 1814 to 230.000 in 1900. In 1850, Christiania overtook [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen "Bergen") and became the most populous city in the country. Christiania expanded its industry from 1840, most importantly around [Akerselva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akerselva "Akerselva"). There was a spectacular building boom during the last decades of the 19th century, with many new apartment buildings and renewal of the city centre, but the boom collapsed in 1899.

In 1877 the city was renamed _Kristiania_.

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Oslo%2C_Carl_Berners_plass_-_no-nb_digifoto_20151113_00218_NB_MIT_FNR_12841B.jpg/250px-Oslo%2C_Carl_Berners_plass_-_no-nb_digifoto_20151113_00218_NB_MIT_FNR_12841B.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oslo,_Carl_Berners_plass_-_no-nb_digifoto_20151113_00218_NB_MIT_FNR_12841B.jpg)

Oslo, 1950s

The city and municipality used the name _Kristiania_ until 1 January 1925 when the original name of _Oslo_[was restored](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographical_renaming "Geographical renaming").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-47) This was because Norway became fully independent in 1905, and Norwegians argued that a name memorializing a Danish king ([Christian IV of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_IV_of_Denmark "Christian IV of Denmark")) was inappropriate as the name of the capital of their country.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-48)

The municipality developed new areas such as [Ullevål garden city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ullev%C3%A5l_Hageby "Ullevål Hageby") (1918–1926) and [Torshov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torshov "Torshov") (1917–1925). [City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_City_Hall "Oslo City Hall") was constructed in the former slum area of [Vika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vika,_Oslo "Vika, Oslo") from 1931 to 1950. In 1948, Oslo merged with [Aker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker,_Norway "Aker, Norway"), a municipality which surrounded the capital and was 27 times larger, thus creating the modern, vastly enlarged Oslo municipality. At the time, Aker was a mostly affluent, green suburban community, and the merger was unpopular in Aker.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-49) Other suburbs, such as [Lambertseter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambertseter "Lambertseter"), began to be developed in the 1950s. [Aker Brygge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker_Brygge "Aker Brygge") was constructed on the site of the former [shipyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipyard "Shipyard"), [Akers Mekaniske Verksted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker_ASA "Aker ASA"), from 1982 to 1998.

Norway was [invaded by Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Weser%C3%BCbung "Operation Weserübung") on 9 April 1940. Efforts to stop the invasion, most notably the [sinking of the _Blücher_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dr%C3%B8bak_Sound "Battle of Drøbak Sound"), delayed the occupation of Oslo for several hours which allowed [King Haakon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haakon_VII_of_Norway "Haakon VII of Norway") to escape the city. Oslo remained occupied throughout the war until Germany capitulated in 1945. During this time, the occupying troops were harried by saboteurs in acts of resistance. On 31 December 1944, allied bombers missed their intended target and hit a [tram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tram "Tram"), resulting in 79 civilian deaths.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-50)

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 21st century")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Oslo_seen_from_Oslofjorden_2022-08-17_43.jpg/250px-Oslo_seen_from_Oslofjorden_2022-08-17_43.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oslo_seen_from_Oslofjorden_2022-08-17_43.jpg)

Oslo, 2022

During the [2011 Norway attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Norway_attacks "2011 Norway attacks"), Oslo was hit by a bomb blast that ripped through the [Government Quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regjeringskvartalet "Regjeringskvartalet"), damaging several buildings including the building that houses the [Office of the Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Prime_Minister_(Norway) "Office of the Prime Minister (Norway)"). Eight people died in the bomb attack.

On 25 June 2022, two people were killed and 21 others injured in [a mass shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Oslo_shooting "2022 Oslo shooting"). An Iranian-born Norwegian citizen was subsequently charged with "aggravated terrorism".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-BBC_News-2022-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-52)

The city has continued to expand. For a few years, new large scale housing areas and infrastructure projects are being built and planned across the city, notably in [Hasle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasle,_Oslo "Hasle, Oslo"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-53)[Helsfyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsfyr "Helsfyr"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-54)[Bjørvika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bj%C3%B8rvika "Bjørvika"),[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-55)[Nydalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nydalen "Nydalen")[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-56) and [Sinsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinsen "Sinsen"), this is increasing the density in and around [Ring 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_2_(Oslo) "Ring 2 (Oslo)") and [Ring 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_3_(Oslo) "Ring 3 (Oslo)"). The [Fornebu line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fornebu_Line "Fornebu Line") on the metro is under construction as of 2024, and further subway lines crossing the inner city are being planned.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-57)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Geography")]

See also: [Oslo Graben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Graben "Oslo Graben")

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Oslo_by_Sentinel-2.jpg/250px-Oslo_by_Sentinel-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oslo_by_Sentinel-2.jpg)

Satellite image of Oslo, July 2018

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Tettstedet_Oslo_2005.png/500px-Tettstedet_Oslo_2005.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tettstedet_Oslo_2005.png)

A map of the urban areas of Oslo in 2005. The grey area in the middle indicates Oslo's city centre.

Oslo occupies an arc of land at the northernmost end of the [Oslofjord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslofjord "Oslofjord"). The [fjord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjord "Fjord"), which is nearly bisected by the [Nesodden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesodden "Nesodden") peninsula opposite Oslo, lies to the south; in all other directions Oslo is surrounded by green hills and mountains. There are 40 islands within the city limits, the largest being [Malmøya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malm%C3%B8ya "Malmøya") (0.56 km 2 or 0.22 sq mi), and scores more around the Oslofjord. Oslo has 343 lakes, the largest being [Maridalsvannet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maridalsvannet "Maridalsvannet") (3.91 km 2 or 1.51 sq mi). This is also a main source of drinking water for large parts of Oslo.

Although [Eastern Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Norway "Eastern Norway") has a number of rivers, none of these flow into the ocean at Oslo. Instead Oslo has two smaller rivers: [Akerselva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akerselva "Akerselva") (draining Maridalsvannet, which flows into the fjord in [Bjørvika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bj%C3%B8rvika "Bjørvika")), and [Alna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alna_River "Alna River"). The waterfalls in Akerselva gave power to some of the first modern industry of Norway in the 1840s. Later in the century, the river became the symbol of the stable and consistent economic and social divide of the city into [an East End and a West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_End_and_West_End_of_Oslo "East End and West End of Oslo"); the labourers' neighbourhoods lie on both sides of the river, and the divide in reality follows Uelands street a bit further west. River Alna flows through Groruddalen, Oslo's major suburb and industrial area. The highest point is Kirkeberget, at 629 m (2,064 ft). Although the city's population is small compared to most European capitals, it occupies an unusually large land area, of which two-thirds are [protected areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_area "Protected area") of forests, hills and lakes. Its boundaries encompass many [parks and open areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parks_and_open_spaces_in_Oslo "Parks and open spaces in Oslo"), giving it an airy and green appearance. ### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Climate")]

Oslo has a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") ([Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): _Dfb_)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-en.climate-data.org-58) or, if the original [Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate "Köppen climate") winter threshold −3°C (27°F) is used, an [oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") (_Cfb_) bordering on a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") in the 1991–2020 base period. Oslo has some of the warmest summers of Norway and fairly cold winters.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-59) Oslo receives a fair amount of precipitation during the year.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-en.climate-data.org-58) The driest seasons are winter and spring, and the wettest are summer and autumn. Because of the city's northern latitude, daylight varies greatly, from more than 18 hours in midsummer, when it never gets completely dark at night (no darker than [nautical twilight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_twilight "Nautical twilight")), to around 6 hours in midwinter.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-60)

The warmest month on record is July 1901 with mean 22.7°C (72.9°F), and the all-time high 35°C (95°F) was also recorded in July 1901.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-61) The warmest month in more recent years is July 2018 with mean 22.2°C (72.0°F) and average daily high 29°C (84.2°F). The record summer of 2018 also recorded the warmest May and May all-time high with 31.1°C (88.0°F) on 30th, and 2018 was even the sunniest year on record with 2133 hours of sunshine.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-63)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-64) On [27 July 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_European_heat_wave "2018 European heat wave"), the temperature in Oslo rose to 34.6°C (94.3°F), the hottest recorded since 1937, when weather recordings started at Blindern. In January, on average three out of four days are below freezing (0°C[32°F]) and one out of four days is colder than −10°C (14°F) (1961–1990).[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-met.no-65) The coldest temperature recorded is −29.6°C (−21.3°F), on 21 January 1841, while the coldest recorded at Blindern is −26°C (−14.8°F) in January 1941. The coldest temperature more recently was on 6 January 2024, where the temperature reached -23.1°C (-17°F) at Oslo-Blindern, which is the coldest measured temperature since January 1987. The coldest month on record is January 1941 and also January 1947 with mean −12.9°C (8.8°F) and average daily low −16.7°C (1.9°F). The average date for the last overnight freeze (low below 0°C, 32.0°F) in spring is 23 April[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-66) and average date for first freeze in autumn is 17 October[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-67) giving a frost-free season of 176 days (1981–2010 average for Blindern). Oslo sits right on the border between [hardiness zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardiness_zones "Hardiness zones") 7a and 7b.

Oslo Gardermoen airport is located 35 km northeast of Oslo and has a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (Köppen climate classification: _Dfb_) bordering on a [subarctic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subarctic_climate "Subarctic climate") (Köppen climate classification: _Dfc_).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-68)

Oslo has many parks and green areas within the city core, as well as outside it.

*   [Frogner Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frogner_Park "Frogner Park") is a large park located a few minutes' walk away from the city centre. This is the biggest and best-known park in Norway, with a large collection of sculptures by [Gustav Vigeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Vigeland "Gustav Vigeland").
*   [Bygdøy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bygd%C3%B8y "Bygdøy") is a large green area, commonly called the Museum Peninsula of Oslo. The area is surrounded by the sea and is one of the most expensive districts in Norway.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-71)
*   [Ekebergparken Sculpture Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekebergparken_Sculpture_Park "Ekebergparken Sculpture Park") is a sculpture park and a national heritage park with a panoramic view of the city at [Ekeberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekeberg "Ekeberg") in the southeast of the city.
*   [St. Hanshaugen Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Hanshaugen_Park "St. Hanshaugen Park") is an old public park on a high hill in central Oslo. "St. Hanshaugen" is also the name of the surrounding neighbourhood as well as the larger administrative district (borough) that includes major parts of central Oslo.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-72)
*   [Tøyen Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%B8yen_Park "Tøyen Park") stretches out behind the old [Munch Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munch_Museum "Munch Museum"), and is a vast, grassy expanse. In the north, there is a lookout point known as Ola Narr. The Tøyen area also includes the [Botanical Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Botanical_Garden_(Oslo) "University Botanical Garden (Oslo)") and Museum belonging to the University of Oslo.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-73)

Oslo (with neighbouring Sandvika-Asker) is built in a horseshoe shape on the shores of the Oslofjord and limited in most directions by hills and forests. As a result, any point within the city is relatively close to the forest. There are two major forests bordering the city: _[Østmarka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98stmarka "Østmarka")_ (literally "Eastern Forest", on the eastern perimeter of the city), and the very large _[Nordmarka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordmarka "Nordmarka")_ (literally "Northern Forest", stretching from the northern perimeter of the city deep into the hinterland).

*   [Sognsvann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sognsvann "Sognsvann") is a lake in Oslomarka, located at the land border, just north of Oslo. Sognsvann was drinking water for Oslo from 1876 to 1967.

The lake's altitude above sea level is 183 metres. The water is in a popular hiking area. Near the water itself, it is great for barbecues, swimming, beach volleyball and other activities.

The municipality operates eight public swimming pools.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-74)[Tøyenbadet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%B8yenbadet "Tøyenbadet") is the largest indoor swimming facility in Oslo and one of the few pools in Norway offering a 50-metre main pool. Another in that size is the outdoor pool [Frognerbadet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frognerbadet "Frognerbadet").

### Architecture

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Fjordbyen.gif/250px-Fjordbyen.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fjordbyen.gif)

[Fjordbyen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fjordbyen "Fjordbyen") is a large construction project in the seaside of central Oslo, stretching from [Bygdøy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bygd%C3%B8y "Bygdøy") in the west to [Ormøya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orm%C3%B8ya "Ormøya") in the east. Some areas include: [Bjørvika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bj%C3%B8rvika "Bjørvika"), [Aker brygge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker_brygge "Aker brygge"), [Tjuvholmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tjuvholmen "Tjuvholmen"), and the [central station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Central_Station "Oslo Central Station") area.

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/A_window_in_Aker_Brygge%2C_Oslo_N.jpg/250px-A_window_in_Aker_Brygge%2C_Oslo_N.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_window_in_Aker_Brygge,_Oslo_N.jpg)

Detail of modern architecture at [Aker Brygge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aker_Brygge "Aker Brygge")

Oslo's architecture is very diverse. The architect [Carl Frederik Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Frederik_Stanley "Carl Frederik Stanley") (1769–1805), who was educated in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), spent some years in Norway around the turn of the 19th century. He undertook some minor commissions for wealthy patrons in and around Oslo, but his major achievement was the renovation of the [Oslo Katedralskole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Katedralskole "Oslo Katedralskole"), completed in 1800.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-76) He added a classical portico to the front of an older structure, and a semicircular auditorium that was sequestered by Parliament in 1814 as a temporary place to assemble, now preserved at [Norsk Folkemuseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norsk_Folkemuseum "Norsk Folkemuseum") as a national monument.

When Christiania was made capital of Norway in 1814, there were practically no buildings suitable for the many new government institutions. An ambitious building program was initiated, but realised very slowly because of economic constraints. The first major undertaking was the [Royal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace,_Oslo "Royal Palace, Oslo"), designed by [Hans Linstow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Linstow "Hans Linstow") and built between 1824 and 1848. Linstow also planned [Karl Johans gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Johans_gate "Karl Johans gate"), the avenue connecting the Palace and the city, with a monumental square halfway to be surrounded by buildings for [University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_University "Oslo University"), the [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stortinget "Stortinget") (Storting) and other institutions. Only the university buildings were realised according to this plan. [Christian Heinrich Grosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Heinrich_Grosch "Christian Heinrich Grosch"), one of the first architects educated completely within Norway, designed the original building for the [Oslo Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Stock_Exchange "Oslo Stock Exchange") (1826–1828), the local branch of the [Bank of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Norway "Bank of Norway") (1828), [Christiania Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christiania_Theatre "Christiania Theatre") (1836–1837), and the first campus for the [University of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oslo "University of Oslo") (1841–1856). For the university buildings, he sought the assistance of the German architect [Karl Friedrich Schinkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel "Karl Friedrich Schinkel"). German architectural influence persisted in Norway, and many wooden buildings followed the principles of [Neoclassicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassicism "Neoclassicism"). In Oslo, the German architect [Alexis de Chateauneuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_de_Chateauneuf "Alexis de Chateauneuf") designed [Trefoldighetskirken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trefoldighetskirken_(Oslo) "Trefoldighetskirken (Oslo)"), the first neo-gothic church, completed by von Hanno in 1858.

A number of landmark buildings, particularly in Oslo, were built in the [Functionalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functionalism_(architecture) "Functionalism (architecture)") style (better known in the US and Britain as Modernist), the first being [Skansen restaurant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skansen_restaurant?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skansen restaurant (page does not exist)")[[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skansen%20restaurant "no:Skansen restaurant")] (1925–1927) by [Lars Backer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lars_Backer "Lars Backer"), demolished in 1970. Backer also designed the restaurant at Ekeberg, which opened in 1929. [Kunstnernes Hus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstnernes_Hus "Kunstnernes Hus") art gallery by [Gudolf Blakstad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudolf_Blakstad "Gudolf Blakstad") and [Herman Munthe-Kaas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Munthe-Kaas "Herman Munthe-Kaas") (1930) still shows the influence of the preceding classicist trend of the 1920s. The redevelopment of [Oslo Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardermoen "Gardermoen") (by the Aviaplan consortium) at Gardermoen, which opened in 1998, was Norway's largest construction project to date.

Oslo is the capital of Norway, and as such is the seat of Norway's national government. Most government offices, including that of the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Norway "Prime Minister of Norway"), are gathered at _Regjeringskvartalet_, a cluster of buildings close to the national Parliament, the [Storting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Norway "Parliament of Norway").

Constituting both a municipality and a county of Norway, the city of Oslo is represented in the Storting by twenty members of parliament. The [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_Norway "Conservative Party of Norway") is the most represented party in Oslo with five members, the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Labour_Party "Norwegian Labour Party") has four, the [Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Norway "Liberal Party of Norway") and the [Socialist Left Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Left_Party_(Norway) "Socialist Left Party (Norway)") have three each; the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_(Norway) "Green Party (Norway)"), the [Red Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Party_(Norway) "Red Party (Norway)") have two each and the [Progress Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_Party_(Norway) "Progress Party (Norway)") has one.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo#cite_note-m595-78)

The combined municipality and county of Oslo has had a [parliamentary system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_system "Parliamentary system") of government since 1986. The supreme authority of the city is the City Council (_Bystyret_), which has 59 seats. Representatives are popularly elected every four years. The city council has five [standing committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_committees "Standing committees"), each having its own areas of responsibility.

### Recent elections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oslo&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Recent elections")]

The largest parties in the City Council after the 2015-elections were the Labour Party and the Conservatives, with 20 and 19 representatives respectively. After 2015, the [city government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government "Local government") was a coalition of the Labour Party, the Green Party and the Socialist Left. With support from the Red Party, the coalition maintained a workable majority in the city council. Following the local elections of 2019, the [centre-left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre-left_politics "Centre-left politics") coalition remained in government until the 2023 local elections.

Cambridge (/ˈkeɪmbrɪdʒ/[3] KAYM-brij) is a city in Middlesex County, Massachusetts, United States. It is located in the Greater Boston metropolitan area directly across the Charles River from Boston. The city's population as of the 2020 U.S. census was 118,403, making it the most populous city in the county, the fourth-largest in Massachusetts behind Boston, Worcester, and Springfield, and ninth-most populous in New England.[4][5] The city was named in honor of the University of Cambridge in Cambridge, England, which was an important center of the Puritan theology that was embraced by the town's founders.[6]: 18 

Founded in December 1630 during the colonial era, Cambridge was one among the first cities established in the Thirteen Colonies, and it went on to play a historic role during the American Revolution. In May 1775, approximately 16,000 American patriots assembled in Cambridge Common to begin organizing a military retaliation against British troops following the Battles of Lexington and Concord. On July 2, 1775, two weeks after the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia formally established the Continental Army and appointed George Washington commander of it, Washington arrived at Cambridge Common to take command of the Patriot soldiers camped there. Many of these soldiers played a role in supporting Washington's successful siege of Boston, which trapped garrisoned British troops from moving by land, forcing the British to ultimately abandon Boston. Cambridge Common is thus celebrated as the birthplace of the Continental Army.[7][8]

Harvard University, an Ivy League university founded in Cambridge in 1636, is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), a private research university, has its 168-acre campus in Cambridge.[9]

Kendall Square, near MIT in the eastern part of Cambridge, has been called "the most innovative square mile on the planet" due to the high concentration of startup companies that have emerged there since 2010.[10] In 2022, Cambridge was home to over 250 biotech companies, with more than 120 located within the Kendall Square ZIP Code.[11]

Pre-colonizationedit

Native Americans inhabited the Charles River basin for thousands of years prior to European colonization of the Americas, as confirmed by archaeological remains in neighboring Watertown and Boston.[12] At the time of European contact, the area was inhabited by Naumkeag of the Pawtucket Confederacy to the north and Massachusett to the south.[13]

The contact period introduced a number of European infectious diseases which would decimate native populations in virgin soil epidemics, significantly depopulating the Charles River basin upon the arrival of large groups of English settlers in the 1630s.[12] A deed for the land that includes present-day Cambridge was ultimately obtained from the Naumkeag Squaw Sachem of Mistick in 1639,[14][15] after a leptospirosis epidemic in 1616–1619[16] and a smallpox epidemic in 1633 killed large portions of her tribe, including two of her sons.[17]

Some sources list Cambridge as the English toponym for Anmoughcawgen, meaning 'fishing weir' or 'beaver dam' in Natick,[18] however this misconception arises from John Smith's 1617 Description of New England,[13][19] in which Cambridge was one of several English place names arbitrarily applied by Smith and Prince Charles I of England,[20][19] in this case to a location on the Kennebec River in Maine,[20] far to the north of the later settlement of Cambridge, which was not so named until 1638.[21] An indigenous place name for the present day location of Cambridge is not known, though other native place names along the Charles in the 1600s included Pequoset and Nonantum upstream and Mishawum and Shawmut downstream,[12][22] while the Charles River (also named by Smith) was known as the Quinobequin.[18]

17th century and colonialismedit

The first settlement of the Massachusetts Bay Colony was established in Salem, in June 1626. That December, the site of present-day Cambridge was chosen for development because it was safely upriver from Boston Harbor, making it easily defensible from attacks by enemy ships. The city was founded by Thomas Dudley, his daughter Anne Bradstreet, and his son-in-law Simon Bradstreet. The first houses were built in the spring of 1631. The settlement was initially referred to as "the newe towne".[23][24] Official Massachusetts records show the name rendered as Newe Towne by 1632, and as Newtowne by 1638.[24][25]

Located at the first convenient Charles River crossing west of Boston, Newtowne was one of several towns, including Boston, Dorchester, Watertown, and Weymouth, founded by the 700 original Puritan colonists of the Massachusetts Bay Colony who arrived on the Winthrop Fleet. Its first preacher was Thomas Hooker, who led many of its original inhabitants west in 1636 to found Hartford and the Connecticut Colony; before leaving, they sold their plots to more recent immigrants from England.[23] The original village site is now within Harvard Square. The marketplace where farmers sold crops from surrounding towns at the edge of a salt marsh (since filled) remains within a small park at the corner of John F. Kennedy and Winthrop Streets.

In 1636, Newe College, later renamed Harvard College after benefactor John Harvard, was founded as North America's first institution of higher learning. Its initial purpose was training ministers. According to Cotton Mather, Newtowne was chosen for the site of the college by the Great and General Court, then the legislature of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, primarily for its proximity to the popular and highly respected Puritan preacher Thomas Shepard. In May 1638,[21] the settlement's name was changed to Cambridge in honor of the University of Cambridge in Cambridge, England.[23][26]

In 1639, the Great and General Court purchased the land that became present-day Cambridge from the Naumkeag Squaw Sachem of Mistick.[14][15]

The town comprised a much larger area than the present city,[23] with various outlying parts becoming independent towns over the years: Cambridge Village (later Newtown and now Newton) in 1688,[27] Cambridge Farms (now Lexington) in 1712[23] or 1713,[28] and Little or South Cambridge (now Brighton)[a] and Menotomy or West Cambridge (now Arlington) in 1807.[23][29][b] In the late 19th century, various schemes for annexing Cambridge to Boston were pursued and rejected.[30]

Newtowne's ministers, Hooker and Shepard, the college's first president, the college's major benefactor, and the first schoolmaster Nathaniel Eaton were all Cambridge alumni, as was the colony's governor John Winthrop. In 1629, Winthrop had led the signing of the founding document of the city of Boston, which was known as the Cambridge Agreement, after the university.[31] In 1650, Governor Thomas Dudley signed the charter creating the corporation that still governs Harvard College.[32]

Cambridge grew slowly as an agricultural village eight miles (13 km) by road from Boston, the colony's capital. By the American Revolution, most residents lived near the Common and Harvard College, with most of the town comprising farms and estates. Most inhabitants were descendants of the original Puritan colonists, but there was also a small elite of Anglican "worthies" who were not involved in village life, made their livings from estates, investments, and trade, and lived in mansions along "the Road to Watertown", present-day Brattle Street, which is still known as Tory Row.

18th century and Revolutionary Waredit

Newly appointed commander-in-chief of the Continental Army General George Washington, dispatched from the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia, arrived on July 3, 1775, and took command of the force of Patriot soldiers camped on Cambridge Common, today regarded as the birthplace of the American army.[23][c]

On January 24, 1776, Henry Knox arrived with an artillery train captured from Fort Ticonderoga, which allowed Washington to force the British Army to evacuate Boston. Most of the Loyalist estates in Cambridge were confiscated after the Revolutionary War.

19th century and industrializationedit

Between 1790 and 1840, Cambridge grew rapidly with the construction of West Boston Bridge in 1792 connecting Cambridge directly to Boston, making it no longer necessary to travel eight miles (13 km) through the Boston Neck, Roxbury, and Brookline to cross the Charles River. A second bridge, the Canal Bridge, opened in 1809 alongside the new Middlesex Canal. The new bridges and roads made what were formerly estates and marshland into prime industrial and residential districts.

In the mid-19th century, Cambridge was the center of a literary revolution. It was home to some of the famous Fireside poets, named because their poems would often be read aloud by families in front of their evening fires. The Fireside poets, including Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, James Russell Lowell, and Oliver Wendell Holmes, were highly popular and influential in this era.

Soon after, turnpikes were built: the Cambridge and Concord Turnpike (today's Broadway and Concord Ave.), the Middlesex Turnpike (Hampshire St. and Massachusetts Ave. northwest of Porter Square), and what are today's Cambridge, Main, and Harvard Streets connected various areas of Cambridge to the bridges. In addition, the town was connected to the Boston & Maine Railroad,[33] leading to the development of Porter Square as well as the creation of neighboring Somerville from the formerly rural parts of Charlestown.

Cambridge was incorporated as a city in 1846.[23] The city's commercial center began to shift from Harvard Square to Central Square, which became the city's downtown around that time.

Between 1850 and 1900, Cambridge took on much of its present character, featuring streetcar suburban development along the turnpikes and working class and industrial neighborhoods focused on East Cambridge, comfortable middle-class housing on the old Cambridgeport, and Mid-Cambridge estates and upper-class enclaves near Harvard University and on the minor hills. The arrival of the railroad in North Cambridge and Northwest Cambridge led to three changes: the development of massive brickyards and brickworks between Massachusetts Avenue, Concord Avenue, and Alewife Brook; the ice-cutting industry launched by Frederic Tudor on Fresh Pond; and the carving up of the last estates into residential subdivisions to house the thousands of immigrants who arrived to work in the new industries.

For much of the 19th and early 20th centuries, the city's largest employer was the New England Glass Company, founded in 1818. By the middle of the 19th century, it was the world's largest and most modern glassworks. In 1888, Edward Drummond Libbey moved all production to Toledo, Ohio, where it continues today under the name Owens-Illinois. The company's flint glassware with heavy lead content is prized by antique glass collectors, and the Toledo Museum of Art has a large collection. The Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and the Sandwich Glass Museum on Cape Cod also house several pieces.

In 1895, Edwin Ginn, founder of Ginn and Company, built the Athenaeum Press Building for his publishing textbook empire.

20th centuryedit

By 1920, Cambridge was one of New England's main industrial cities, with nearly 120,000 residents. Among the largest businesses in Cambridge during the period of industrialization was Carter's Ink Company, whose neon sign long adorned the Charles River and which was for many years the world's largest ink manufacturer. Next door was the Athenaeum Press. Confectionery and snack manufacturers in the Cambridgeport-Area 4-Kendall corridor included Kennedy Biscuit Factory, later part of Nabisco and originator of the Fig Newton,[34] Necco, Squirrel Brands,[35] George Close Company (1861–1930s),[36] Page & Shaw, Daggett Chocolate (1892–1960s, recipes bought by Necco),[37] Fox Cross Company (1920–1980, originator of the Charleston Chew, and now part of Tootsie Roll Industries),[38] Kendall Confectionery Company, and James O. Welch (1927–1963, originator of Junior Mints, Sugar Daddies, Sugar Mamas, and Sugar Babies, now part of Tootsie Roll Industries).[39] Main Street was nicknamed "Confectioner's Row".[40]

Only the Cambridge Brands subsidiary of Tootsie Roll Industries remains in town, still manufacturing Junior Mints in the old Welch factory on Main Street.[39] The Blake and Knowles Steam Pump Company (1886), the Kendall Boiler and Tank Company (1880, now in Chelmsford, Massachusetts), and the New England Glass Company (1818–1878) were among the industrial manufacturers in what are now Kendall Square and East Cambridge.

In 1935, the Cambridge Housing Authority and the Public Works Administration demolished an integrated low-income tenement neighborhood with African Americans and European immigrants. In its place, it built the whites-only "Newtowne Court" public housing development and the adjoining, blacks-only "Washington Elms" project in 1940; the city required segregation in its other public housing projects as well.[41][42][43]

As industry in New England began to decline during the Great Depression and after World War II, Cambridge lost much of its industrial base. It also began to become an intellectual, rather than an industrial, center. Harvard University, which had always been important as both a landowner and an institution, began to play a more dominant role in the city's life and culture. When Radcliffe College was established in 1879, the town became a mecca for some of the nation's most academically talented female students. MIT's move from Boston to Cambridge in 1916 reinforced Cambridge's status as an intellectual center of the United States.

After the 1950s, the city's population began to decline slowly as families tended to be replaced by single people and young couples. In Cambridge Highlands, the technology company Bolt, Beranek, & Newman produced the first network router in 1969 and hosted the invention of computer-to-computer email in 1971. The 1980s brought a wave of high technology startups. Those selling advanced minicomputers were overtaken by the microcomputer.[citation needed][44] Cambridge-based VisiCorp made the first spreadsheet software for personal computers, VisiCalc, and helped propel the Apple II to consumer success. It was overtaken and purchased by Cambridge-based Lotus Development, maker of Lotus 1-2-3 (which was, in turn, replaced in by Microsoft Excel).

The city continues to be home to many startups. Kendall Square was a software hub through the dot-com boom and today hosts offices of such technology companies as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon. The Square also now houses the headquarters of Akamai.[45]

In 1976, Harvard's plans to start experiments with recombinant DNA led to a three-month moratorium and a citizen review panel. In the end, Cambridge decided to allow such experiments but passed safety regulations in 1977. This led to regulatory certainty and acceptance when Biogen opened a lab in 1982, in contrast to the hostility that caused the Genetic Institute, a Harvard spinoff, to abandon Somerville and Boston for Cambridge.[46] The biotech and pharmaceutical industries have since thrived in Cambridge, which now includes headquarters for Biogen and Genzyme; laboratories for Novartis, Teva, Takeda, Alnylam, Ironwood, Moderna Therapeutics, Editas Medicine; support companies such as Cytel; and many smaller companies.

Rent controledit
See also: Rent control in Cambridge, Massachusetts

During the era of rent control in Massachusetts, at least 20 percent of all rent controlled apartments in Cambridge housed high-income earners, with the majority housing people with professional, technical, and managerial jobs.[47][48][49] In an independent study conducted of 2/3 of the rent controlled apartments in Cambridge in 1988, 246 were households headed by doctors, 298 by lawyers, 265 by architects, 259 by professors, and 220 by engineers.[47] There were 2,650 with students, including 1,503 with graduate students.[47]

Those who lived in rent controlled apartments included

Ruth Abrams, a Justice of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court.[50][47][49][d]
Kenneth Reeves, the mayor of Cambridge at the time rent control was repealed in Massachusetts, was living in the same rent controlled apartment he lived in as a Harvard student in 1973.[47][e]
Frederik, Crown Prince of Denmark[51][47]

The end of rent control in 1994 had numerous effects on the city. Within four years of repealing the law, Cambridge, where "the city's form of rent control was unusually strict," saw new housing and construction increase by 50%, and the tax revenue from construction permits tripled.[51] Property values in Cambridge increased by about $7.8 billion in the decade following the repeal.[52] Roughly a quarter of this increase, $1.8 billion ($3 billion in 2024 dollars), was due to the repeal of rent control.[52]

Close to 40% of all Cambridge properties were under rent control when it was repealed.[52] Their property values appreciated faster than non-rent controlled properties, as did the properties around them.[53] By the end of the 20th century, Cambridge had one of the most costly housing markets in the Northeastern United States.[54]

21st centuryedit

Cambridge's mix of amenities and proximity to Boston kept housing prices relatively stable despite the bursting of the United States housing bubble in 2008 and 2009.[55] Cambridge has been a sanctuary city since 1985 and reaffirmed its status as such in 2006.[56]

Geographyedit
A winter view of Cambridge and Harvard University's Weld Boathouse seen from Boston with the Charles River in the foreground

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Cambridge has a total area of 7.1 square miles (18 km2), 6.4 square miles (17 km2) of which is land and 0.7 square miles (1.8 km2) (9.82%) of which is water.

Adjacent municipalitiesedit

Cambridge is located in eastern Massachusetts, bordered by:

the city of Boston to the south and east (across the Charles River)
the neighborhood of Charlestown to the east
the city of Somerville to the north
the town of Arlington to the northwest
the town of Belmont and
the city of Watertown to the west

The border between Cambridge and the neighboring city of Somerville passes through densely populated neighborhoods, which are connected by the MBTA Red Line. Some of the main squares, Inman, Porter, and to a lesser extent, Harvard and Lechmere, are very close to the city line, as are Somerville's Union and Davis Squares.

Through the City of Cambridge's exclusive municipal water system, the city further controls two exclave areas, one being Payson Park Reservoir and Gatehouse, a 2009 listed American Water Landmark located roughly one mile west of Fresh Pond and surrounded by the town of Belmont. The second area is the larger Hobbs Brook and Stony Brook watersheds, which share borders with neighboring towns and cities including Lexington, Lincoln, Waltham and Weston.

Squaresedit

Cambridge has been called the "City of Squares",[57] as most of its commercial districts are major street intersections known as squares. Each square acts as a neighborhood center.

Kendall Square, formed by the junction of Broadway, Main Street, and Third Street, has been called "the most innovative square mile on the planet", owing to its high concentration of entrepreneurial start-ups and quality of innovation which have emerged in the vicinity of the square since 2010.[10][58] Technology Square is an office and laboratory building cluster in this neighborhood. Just over the Longfellow Bridge from Boston, at the eastern end of the MIT campus, it is served by the Kendall/MIT station on the MBTA Red Line subway. Most of Cambridge's large office towers are located in the Square. Kendall Square houses some of the biggest technological companies of the world, including Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Apple. A biotech industry has developed in this area. The Cambridge Innovation Center, a large co-working space, is in Kendall Square at 1 Broadway. The Cambridge Center office complex is in Kendall Square, and not at the actual center of Cambridge. The "One Kendall Square" complex is nearby, but not actually in Kendall Square.

Central Square is formed by the junction of Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street, and Western Avenue.[59]: 1  Containing a variety of ethnic restaurants, it was economically depressed as recently as the late 1990s; it underwent gentrification in recent years (in conjunction with the development of the nearby University Park at MIT), and continues to grow more costly.[60] It is served by the Central Square stop on the MBTA Red Line subway.[59]: 1–2  Lafayette Square, formed by the junction of Massachusetts Avenue, Columbia Street, Sidney Street, and Main Street, is considered part of the Central Square area. Cambridgeport is south of Central Square, and bordered by MIT, the Charles River, Massachusetts Avenue, and River Street.[61]

Harvard Square is formed by the junction of Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street, Dunster Street, and JFK Street.[62] This is the primary site of Harvard University and a major Cambridge shopping area.[62] It is served by the Harvard Square Red Line station.[63] Harvard Square was originally the Red Line's northwestern terminus and a major transfer point to streetcars that also operated in a short tunnel—which is still a major bus terminal, although the area under the Square was reconfigured dramatically in the 1980s when the Red Line was extended.[64] A short distance away from the square lies the Cambridge Common, while the neighborhood north of Harvard and east of Massachusetts Avenue is known as Baldwin, in honor of the first Black principal of Cambridge public schools, Maria L. Baldwin. It was renamed "Baldwin" in 2021, and so some know the area better by its former name, Agassiz, after the famed scientist Louis Agassiz.[65][66][67]

Porter Square is about a mile north on Massachusetts Avenue from Harvard Square, at the junction of Massachusetts and Somerville Avenues.[68] It includes part of the city of Somerville[citation needed] and is served by the Porter Square Station, a complex housing a Red Line stop and a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.[69] Lesley University's University Hall and Porter campus are in Porter Square.[citation needed]

Inman Square is at the junction of Cambridge and Hampshire streets in mid-Cambridge.[70] It is home to restaurants, bars, music venues, and boutiques.[70] Victorian streetlights, benches, and bus stops were added to the streets in the 2000s, and a new city park was installed.[citation needed]

Lechmere Square is at the junction of Cambridge and First streets, adjacent to the CambridgeSide Galleria shopping mall. It is served by Lechmere station on the MBTA Green Line.[71]

Other neighborhoodsedit

The City of Cambridge officially recognizes 13 neighborhoods, which are as follows:

East Cambridge (Area 1) is bordered on the north by Somerville, on the east by the Charles River, on the south by Broadway and Main Street, and on the west by the Grand Junction Railroad tracks. It includes the NorthPoint development.
MIT Campus (Area 2) is bordered on the north by Broadway, on the south and east by the Charles River, and on the west by the Grand Junction Railroad tracks.
Wellington-Harrington (Area 3) is bordered on the north by Somerville, on the south and west by Hampshire Street, and on the east by the Grand Junction Railroad tracks.
The Port, formerly known as Area 4, is bordered on the north by Hampshire Street, on the south by Massachusetts Avenue, on the west by Prospect Street, and on the east by the Grand Junction Railroad tracks. Residents of Area 4 often simply call their neighborhood "The Port" and the area of Cambridgeport and Riverside "The Coast". In October 2015, the Cambridge City Council officially renamed Area 4 "The Port", formalizing the longtime nickname, largely on the initiative of neighborhood native and then-Vice Mayor Dennis Benzan.[72]
Cambridgeport (Area 5) is bordered on the north by Massachusetts Avenue, on the south by the Charles River, on the west by River Street, and on the east by the Grand Junction Railroad tracks.
Mid-Cambridge (Area 6) is bordered on the north by Kirkland and Hampshire Streets and Somerville, on the south by Massachusetts Avenue, on the west by Peabody Street, and on the east by Prospect Street.
Riverside (Area 7), an area sometimes called "The Coast", is bordered on the north by Massachusetts Avenue, on the south by the Charles River, on the west by JFK Street, and on the east by River Street.
Baldwin (Area 8) is bordered on the north by Somerville, on the south and east by Kirkland Street, and on the west by Massachusetts Avenue.
Neighborhood Nine or Radcliffe (formerly called Peabody, until the recent relocation of a neighborhood school by that name) is bordered on the north by railroad tracks, on the south by Concord Avenue, on the west by railroad tracks, and on the east by Massachusetts Avenue. The Avon Hill sub-neighborhood consists of the higher elevations within the area bounded by Upland Road, Raymond Street, Linnaean Street and Massachusetts Avenue.
West Cambridge (Area 10) is bordered on the north by Concord Avenue and Garden Street, on the south by the Charles River and Watertown, on the west by Fresh Pond and the Collins Branch Library, and on the east by JFK Street. It includes the sub-neighborhoods of Brattle Street (formerly known as Tory Row) and Huron Village.
North Cambridge (Area 11) is bordered on the north by Arlington and Somerville, on the south by railroad tracks, on the west by Belmont, and on the east by Somerville.
Cambridge Highlands (Area 12) is bordered on the north and east by railroad tracks, on the south by Fresh Pond, and on the west by Belmont.
Strawberry Hill (Area 13) is bordered on the north by Fresh Pond, on the south by Watertown, on the west by Belmont, and on the east by the Watertown-Cambridge Greenway (formerly railroad tracks).

Climateedit

In the Köppen-Geiger classification, Cambridge has a hot-summer humid continental climate (Dfa) with four well-defined seasons. Summers are warm to hot, fall and spring are cool and rainy, and winter is cold and gray with occasional snowstorms. Abundant rain falls on the city (and in the winter often as snow); it has no dry season. The average January temperature is 26.6 °F (−3 °C), making Cambridge part of Group D, independent of the isotherm.[73]

As of the census[98] of 2010, there were 105,162 people, 44,032 households, and 17,420 families residing in the city. The population density was 16,354.9 inhabitants per square mile (6,314.7/km2). There were 47,291 housing units at an average density of 7,354.7 per square mile (2,839.7/km2). The racial makeup of the city was 66.60% White, 11.70% Black or African American, 0.20% Native American, 15.10% Asian (3.7% Chinese, 1.4% Asian Indian, 1.2% Korean, 1.0% Japanese[99]), 0.01% Pacific Islander, 2.10% from other races, and 4.30% from two or more races. 7.60% of the population were Hispanic or Latino of any race (1.6% Puerto Rican, 1.4% Mexican, 0.6% Dominican, 0.5% Colombian & Salvadoran, 0.4% Spaniard). Non-Hispanic Whites were 62.1% of the population in 2010,[92] down from 89.7% in 1970.[93] An individual resident of Cambridge is known as a Cantabrigian.

In 2010, there were 44,032 households, out of which 16.9% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 28.9% were married couples living together, 8.4% had a female householder with no husband present, and 60.4% were non-families. 40.7% of all households were made up of individuals, and 9.6% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.00 and the average family size was 2.76.

In the city, the population was spread out, with 13.3% of the population under the age of 18, 21.2% from 18 to 24, 38.6% from 25 to 44, 17.8% from 45 to 64, and 9.2% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 30.5 years. For every 100 females, there were 96.1 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 94.7 males.

The median income for a household in the city was $47,979, and the median income for a family was $59,423 (these figures had risen to $58,457 and $79,533 respectively as of a 2007 estimate[100]). Males had a median income of $43,825 versus $38,489 for females. The per capita income for the city was $31,156. About 8.7% of families and 12.9% of the population were below the poverty line, including 15.1% of those under age 18 and 12.9% of those age 65 or over.

Locals living in and near the city jokingly refer to it as "The People's Republic of Cambridge".[101] For 2016, the residential property tax rate in Cambridge was $6.99 per $1,000.[102] Cambridge enjoys the highest possible bond credit rating, AAA, with all three Wall Street rating agencies.[103]

In 2000, 11.0% of city residents were of Irish ancestry; 7.2% were of English, 6.9% Italian, 5.5% West Indian and 5.3% German ancestry. 69.4% spoke only English at home, while 6.9% spoke Spanish, 3.2% Chinese or Mandarin, 3.0% Portuguese, 2.9% French Creole, 2.3% French, 1.5% Korean, and 1.0% Italian.

Economyedit
Kendall Square, the center of Cambridge's biotech economy as seen from the Charles River

Manufacturing was an important part of Cambridge's economy in the late 19th and early 20th century. Major employers in Cambridge include the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard University which together employ over 23,000 individuals, as well as the Cambridge Innovation Center, the City of Cambridge, and biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies including Takeda Pharmaceuticals, Biogen, Novartis, Moderna, and Sanofi.[105] Since the late 20th century, Kendall Square and adjacent areas have shifted from primarily industrial uses toward biotechnology, laboratory, office, and mixed-use development. As a cradle of technological innovation, Cambridge was home to technology firms Analog Devices, Akamai, Bolt, Beranek, and Newman (BBN Technologies) (now part of Raytheon), General Radio (later GenRad), Lotus Development Corporation (now part of IBM), Polaroid, Symbolics, and Thinking Machines.

In 1996, Polaroid, Arthur D. Little, and Lotus were Cambridge's top employers, with over 1,000 employees, but they faded out a few years later. Health care and biotechnology firms such as Genzyme, Biogen Idec, bluebird bio, Millennium Pharmaceuticals, Sanofi, Pfizer and Novartis[106] have significant presences in the city. Though headquartered in Switzerland, Novartis continues to expand its operations in Cambridge. Other major biotech and pharmaceutical firms expanding their presence in Cambridge include GlaxoSmithKline, AstraZeneca, Shire, and Pfizer.[107] Most of Cambridge's biotech firms are in Kendall Square and East Cambridge, which decades ago were the city's center of manufacturing. Some others are in University Park at MIT, a new development in another former manufacturing area.[108][109]

None of the high technology firms that once dominated the economy was among the 25 largest employers in 2005, but by 2008 Akamai and ITA Software were.[110] Google,[111] IBM Research, Microsoft Research, and Philips Research[112] maintain offices in Cambridge. In late January 2012—less than a year after acquiring Billerica-based analytic database management company, Vertica—Hewlett-Packard announced it would also be opening its first offices in Cambridge.[113] Also around that time, e-commerce giants Staples[114] and Amazon.com[115] said they would be opening research and innovation centers in Kendall Square. And LabCentral provides a shared laboratory facility for approximately 25 emerging biotech companies.[116][117][unreliable source?]

The proximity of Cambridge's universities has also made the city a center for nonprofit groups and think tanks, including the National Bureau of Economic Research, the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, Cultural Survival, and Science Club for Girls.[citation needed]

In September 2011, Cambridge launched its Entrepreneur Walk of Fame initiative, recognizing people who have made contributions to innovation in global business.[118]

In 2021, Cambridge was one of approximately 27 US cities to receive a AAA rating from each of the three major US credit rating agencies, Moody's Investors Service, Standard & Poor's and Fitch Ratings. 2021 marked the 22nd consecutive year that Cambridge had retained this distinction.[119] Cambridge's massive tax base has allowed it to keep residential taxes fairly low, and its budget is the second largest in the state despite being the fourth largest in population.[120][121]

Public artedit

Cambridge has a large and varied collection of permanent public art, on both city property, managed by the Cambridge Arts Council,[123] Community Art Center,[124] and the Harvard[125] and MIT[126] campuses. Temporary public artworks are displayed as part of the annual Cambridge River Festival on the banks of the Charles River during winter celebrations in Harvard and Central Squares and at Harvard University campus sites. Experimental forms of public artistic and cultural expression include the Central Square World's Fair, the annual Somerville-based Honk! Festival,[127] and If This House Could Talk,[128] a neighborhood art and history event.

Street musicians and other performers entertain tourists and locals in Harvard Square during the warmer months. The performances are coordinated through a public process that has been developed collaboratively by the performers,[129] city administrators, private organizations and business groups.[130] The Cambridge public library contains four Works Progress Administration murals completed in 1935 by Elizabeth Tracy Montminy: Religion, Fine Arts, History of Books and Paper, and The Development of the Printing Press.[131]

Parks and recreationedit
Alewife Brook Reservation

Consisting largely of densely built residential space, Cambridge lacks significant tracts of public parkland. Easily accessible open space on the university campuses, including Harvard Yard, Radcliffe Yard, and MIT's Great Lawn, as well as the considerable open space of Mount Auburn Cemetery and Fresh Pond Reservation, partly compensates for this. At Cambridge's western edge, the cemetery is known as a garden cemetery because of its landscaping (the oldest planned landscape in the country) and arboretum. Although known as a Cambridge landmark, much of the cemetery lies within Watertown.[133] It is also an Important Bird Area (IBA) in the Greater Boston area. Fresh Pond Reservation is the largest open green space in Cambridge with 162 acres (656,000 m2) of land around a 155-acre (627,000 m2) kettle hole lake. This land includes a 2.25-mile walking trail around the reservoir and a public nine-hole golf course.[134]

Public parkland includes the esplanade along the Charles River, which mirrors its Boston counterpart, Cambridge Common, Danehy Park, and Alewife Brook Reservation.

The 5th district seat is held by Democrat Katherine Clark, who replaced now-Senator Ed Markey in a 2013 special election; the 7th is represented by Democrat Ayanna Pressley, elected in 2018. The state's senior United States senator is Democrat Elizabeth Warren, elected in 2012, who lives in Cambridge. The governor of Massachusetts is Democrat Maura Healey, elected in 2022.

Cambridge is represented in six districts in the Massachusetts House of Representatives: the 24th Middlesex (which includes parts of Belmont and Arlington), the 25th and 26th Middlesex (the latter of which includes a portion of Somerville), the 29th Middlesex (which includes a small part of Watertown), and the Eighth and Ninth Suffolk (both including parts of the City of Boston).[137] The city is represented in the Massachusetts Senate as a part of the 2nd Middlesex, Middlesex and Suffolk, and 1st Suffolk and Middlesex districts.[138]

Politicsedit

From 1860 to 1880, Republicans Abraham Lincoln, Ulysses S. Grant, Rutherford B. Hayes, and James Garfield each won Cambridge, Grant doing so by margins of over 20 points in both of his campaigns. Following that, from 1884 to 1892, Grover Cleveland won Cambridge in all three of his presidential campaigns, by less than ten points each time.

Then from 1896 to 1924, Cambridge became something of a swing city with a slight Republican lean. Republican candidates carried the city in five of the eight presidential elections during that time, with five of the elections resulting in either a plurality or a margin of victory of fewer than ten points. In modern times, however, Cambridge has been a stronghold of the Democratic Party due to the increasingly leftward shift of college towns, and has gained nicknames such as the "People's Republic of Cambridge" or "Berkeley on the Charles." While Cambridge's policies are not uniformly left-wing (for example, it has the lowest property tax in metro Boston), Republicans represent a tiny minority in Cambridge, and Democratic incumbents frequently run either unopposed or opposed by fellow Democrats.[139]

In the last 23 presidential elections, dating back to the nomination of Al Smith in the 1928 presidential election, Democratic presidential candidates have won Cambridge with every Democratic nominee since Massachusetts native John F. Kennedy in 1960 receiving at least 70% of the vote, except for Jimmy Carter in 1976 and 1980. Since 1928, the only Republican nominee to come within ten points of carrying Cambridge is Dwight Eisenhower in his 1956 reelection bid. At the state level, Cambridge has consistently delivered its vote to the Democratic Party even during overwhelming Republican sweeps, such as Bill Weld's 1994 re-election (during which Cambridge was the only municipality in all of eastern Massachusetts to vote Democrat) and Charlie Baker's 2018 re-election. Cambridge has consistently voted for left-wing causes, such as ranked-choice voting, marijuana legalization, and physician-assisted suicide.

City governmentedit

Cambridge City Hall in the 1980s

Cambridge has a city government led by a mayor and a nine-member city council. There is also a six-member school committee that functions alongside the superintendent of public schools. The councilors and school committee members are elected every two years using proportional representation.[171]

The mayor is elected by the city councilors from among themselves and serves as the chair of city council meetings. The mayor also sits on the school committee. The mayor is not the city's chief executive. Rather, the city manager, who is appointed by the city council, serves in that capacity.

Under the city's Plan E form of government, the city council does not have the power to appoint or remove city officials who are under the direction of the city manager. The city council and its members are also forbidden from giving orders to any subordinate of the city manager.[173]

Yi-An Huang is the City Manager as of September 6, 2022, succeeding Owen O'Riordan (now the Deputy City Manager) who briefly served as the Acting City Manager after Louis DePasquale resigned on July 5, 2022, after six years in office.[174]

County governmentedit

Cambridge was a county seat of Middlesex County, along with Lowell, until the abolition of executive county government. Though the county government was abolished in 1997, the county still exists as a geographical and political region.[175] The employees of Middlesex County courts, jails, registries, and other county agencies are now employed directly by the Commonwealth. The county's registry of Deeds remain in Cambridge, but the Probate and Family Court, Superior Court, District Attorney's and Sheriff's offices have had their operations transferred roughly nine miles north to Woburn.[176][177] The local Third District Court has shifted operations to Medford.[178] The Middlesex County Jail & House of Correction was also relocated 25 miles north from Cambridge to Billerica in 2014.[179]
